title: Consider the lilies (Luke 12:22–34)
hook: the ravens don't sow, the lilies don't spin

segments.voice: Yesterday, a farmer built bigger barns and didn't get one evening to enjoy them. Your line was this night. What did you give away? Day four hundred sixty-four.

Two in the morning, and the ceiling has become very interesting. Rent, a test result, a child who hasn't texted back, the thing said at work that can't be unsaid. Worry doesn't keep office hours. Right after the story of the rich man and his barns, Jesus turns to his own disciples, people who have no barns at all, and talks about exactly this. He doesn't give them a budget. He tells them to look at two things: a bird and a flower. Today, the ravens and the lilies.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `WORRY KEEPS NO OFFICE HOURS.` → `A BIRD AND A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Jesus says: be not solicitous for your life, what you'll eat, or for your body, what you'll wear. Solicitous is the Douay's word for anxious. Then the first picture: "Consider the ravens, for they sow not, neither do they reap, neither have they storehouse nor barn, and God feedeth them." No barn. That's a pointed word right after yesterday. And Luke says ravens, where Matthew says simply the birds of the air. The raven was a scavenger, a noisy black bird, and the Law of Moses listed it among the birds not to be eaten. Not a pretty bird. God feeds it anyway. Then the second picture: "Consider the lilies, how they grow: they labour not, neither do they spin." Spinning thread was daily work, the way people made cloth. The lilies make nothing, and yet Solomon in all his glory wasn't dressed like one of them. Which flower did Jesus mean? The text doesn't say, and nobody knows for sure. Readers have guessed anemones, irises and others. Then the punch line: which of you, by taking thought, can add to his stature one cubit? Worry doesn't add anything. And then a tender line: fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you a kingdom. So sell what you have, give alms, and make purses that don't wear out. Because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Consider is the key word. It means look closely, study, take your time. Jesus doesn't argue people out of worry. He asks them to look at something alive and let it teach them.
screen: `BE NOT SOLICITOUS: DON'T BE ANXIOUS.` · `RAVENS: NO STOREHOUSE, NO BARN.` · `LILIES: THEY NEITHER LABOR NOR SPIN.` · `FEAR NOT, LITTLE FLOCK.` · then, large: `CONSIDER THE LILIES, HOW THEY GROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a flower and stop worrying. If you can, find a real one: a houseplant, a weed in a crack, a picture on your phone if that's all you have. Settle, and breathe. Now consider it, the way Jesus said: slowly. The color at the center. The way the petals are folded. How it's simply being what it is. When a worry walks in, notice it, and gently bring your eyes back to the flower. If you pray, let it remind you who clothes it. The bell holds the time.
Consider the lilies. Jesus' cure for anxiety: look closely at ravens with no barns and flowers that never spin, and remember who feeds and clothes them. Today's word.
Your line: consider the lilies. Today, when worry starts to spin, stop and look closely at one living thing for ten seconds. Day four hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this teaching on anxiety in the Gospel readings at Mass, and some pray with it when they speak of trusting God's providence, his care for all he has made.

fork.setup: your disciples are anxious about food and clothes, and they have no barns. what do you tell them first?
options: make a careful plan for the winter.
look at the ravens and the lilies.
work harder so you won't worry.
fork.reveal: he tells them to consider the ravens and the lilies, then: fear not, little flock.

original.note: Greek: consider the lilies. The verb means look closely, take it in, study it.

trapdoor: what you thought: consider the lilies means don't plan anything.
what it means: Jesus asks anxious people to look closely at God's care for ravens and flowers, and to set their hearts on the kingdom.
what a scholar hears: Luke says ravens (korakas), birds the Law listed as unclean (Leviticus 11:15), where Matthew says birds of the air.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer claims 'many people know' the scene; cut unsourced spring-wildflowers claim and 'scholars have guessed' (now 'readers'); 'by worrying' paraphrase brought to the Douay's 'by taking thought'; dropped 'gentlest line' superlative; howItsDone no longer makes an unsourced claim about Franciscan communities.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 12:24 and 12:27, and 'be not solicitous' in 12:22.
Ravens among birds not to be eaten (Leviticus 11:15; Deuteronomy 14:14): confirm.
Identification of the lilies is uncertain; anemones and irises are common guesses. Confirm phrasing.
Luke 12:25 'add to his stature one cubit' is paraphrased as 'one cubit to his height'; some read it as adding time to one's life. Consider noting.
